parts.title: Part I - Understanding the execution problem
parts.purpose: The reader first learns what an execution algorithm is trying to accomplish, how a market absorbs orders, and what it means to say that an execution was expensive.

chapters.title: The Execution Problem
chapters.purpose: Frames execution as a decision problem in which inventory must be traded while prices, liquidity, and information continue to change.
chapters.subtopics: Parent and child orders; inventory dynamics and trading rate; market state, information, and admissible policies; implementation shortfall and terminal completion; immediacy, impact, price risk, and alpha decay; benchmarks and constraints; open-loop schedules and feedback policies; partial observation; Bellman recursion and the HJB equation; prediction, causal response, and control; model risk, units, and normalization.

chapters.title: How Markets Absorb Orders
chapters.purpose: Builds an economic picture of the trading venue before reducing liquidity to a handful of model inputs.
chapters.subtopics: The bid, ask, spread, and depth; marketable and resting limit orders; price-time priority and queue position; book-walking cost; spread capture and adverse selection; fill and non-fill value; trade and order-flow imbalance; microprice; mechanical, informational, and common-cause price response; hidden liquidity and cancellations; replenishment and resilience; liquidity across horizons; calendar, event, and volume time; intraday seasonality; fragmentation and routing; dark liquidity; auctions; translating mechanism into control state.

chapters.title: What Does an Execution Cost?
chapters.purpose: Defines the outcomes that execution research tries to explain and shows why the benchmark determines the economic question.
chapters.subtopics: Arrival-price implementation shortfall; VWAP, TWAP, close, and interval benchmarks; spread cost; timing risk; impact; opportunity cost; markouts; partial fills and unfinished orders; realized versus expected cost; cost decomposition; counterfactual interpretation; transaction-cost analysis.

parts.title: Part II - Learning from execution data
parts.purpose: This part develops the research judgment needed to turn market observations into defensible measurements, models, and forecasts.

chapters.title: Statistical Modeling as a Research Process
chapters.purpose: Explains how to move from an observed market phenomenon to a model that can support an explanation, forecast, or decision.
chapters.subtopics: Research-question formation; the phenomenon, population, observational unit, target, and estimand; data-generating stories; prediction, explanation, causal estimation, and control; information available at decision time; data contracts; noisy labels; feature mechanisms and invariances; validation design; model ladders; bias, variance, and irreducible noise; learning curves; residual analysis; uncertainty; extrapolation; distribution shift; decision-aware evaluation; research logs and synthetic experiments.

chapters.title: Execution Data: From Market Events to Research Tables
chapters.purpose: Shows how orders, fills, quotes, and trades become a trustworthy research dataset without losing their timing or economic meaning.
chapters.subtopics: Order, fill, quote, trade, and depth records; entity keys and order lifecycles; sequence numbers and book replay; parent-order reconstruction; event alignment and latency-aware quote matching; timestamps and clock synchronization; calendar, event, and volume-time sampling; stale observations; missingness; cancellations and censored fills; corporate actions and effective-dated reference data; futures rolls and exact contract identity; live versus corrected data; leakage-safe joins; data lineage, reconciliation, and reproducible research tables.

chapters.title: The Empirical Shape of Market Impact
chapters.purpose: Describes the regularities seen in execution data before imposing a particular functional form or causal interpretation.
chapters.subtopics: Signed response and the missing no-trade path; child-order and parent-order scales; clock and quantity-progress trajectories; order size, intended and realized participation, and duration; concavity and square-root behavior; average, total, and marginal cost; temporary, transient, and permanent horizons; pauses, resilience, and post-trade decay; mechanical and informational response; volatility, spread, depth, and volume normalization; time-of-day effects; regimes and cross-sectional collapse; equities, futures, options, and less-liquid products; futures rolls; exploratory surface diagnostics; translation from empirical regularity to control input.

chapters.title: Estimating Market Impact
chapters.purpose: Develops statistical methods for estimating impact while being explicit about selection, endogeneity, uncertainty, and model use.
chapters.subtopics: Parametric and nonparametric specifications; log-log models; nonlinear and constrained regression; heteroskedasticity and heavy tails; hierarchical shrinkage; interactions and segmentation; metaorder reconstruction; endogenous participation and duration; latent urgency; confounding and selection; measurement error; causal designs; uncertainty intervals; stability; residual diagnostics; policy sensitivity.

chapters.title: Short-Horizon Forecasting and Liquidity State
chapters.purpose: Forecasts the market quantities that distinguish execution actions, including both liquidity conditions and short-lived price pressure.
chapters.subtopics: Decision horizons and action-conditional forecasts; intraday and remaining-day volume distributions; intended and realized participation; spread and depth transitions; book-walking cost; realized and forecast volatility; inventory-weighted forecast loss; imbalance, microprice, and order-flow imbalance; multi-horizon price and markout prediction; alpha decay and value net of execution cost; fill probability and fill-conditioned adverse selection; event intensities and point processes; state-space and latent-liquidity models; regime switching; trees, boosting, neural networks, and Gaussian processes; joint probabilistic forecasts; calibration; scenario generation; temporal leakage; forecast value for control; drift and fallback.

parts.title: Part III - From estimated models to execution policies
parts.purpose: The emphasis now moves from describing costs and market state to choosing actions and understanding why an optimal policy behaves as it does.

chapters.title: Classical Optimal Liquidation
chapters.purpose: Derives the basic cost-risk trade-off and uses it to explain the shape of an optimal liquidation schedule.
chapters.subtopics: Discrete and continuous inventory dynamics; temporary impact; price risk; Bertsimas-Lo; Almgren-Chriss; expected cost and variance; the execution frontier; risk aversion and urgency; boundary conditions; closed-form trajectories; calibration; units and limiting cases; when the classical assumptions fail.

chapters.title: Volume Time, VWAP, and Participation Strategies
chapters.purpose: Connects optimal liquidation to the schedules and constraints used by practical execution algorithms.
chapters.subtopics: Calendar time and volume time; TWAP and VWAP schedules; constant and time-varying POV; uncertain future volume; participation caps and floors; completion constraints; catch-up logic near deadlines; benchmark-aware control; realized versus intended participation; interaction among impact, volume forecasts, and alpha decay.

chapters.title: Transient Impact and Market Resilience
chapters.purpose: Introduces impact with memory and studies how liquidity recovery changes the value of waiting and the shape of a schedule.
chapters.subtopics: Propagator states; exponential and power-law kernels; resilience; path-dependent execution cost; child-order spacing; post-trade decay; kernel estimation; mechanical decay versus informational reversion; price manipulation; no-dynamic-arbitrage restrictions; optimal schedules under transient impact.

chapters.title: Adaptive Execution
chapters.purpose: Explains how a policy should respond when forecasts, market conditions, or beliefs change during an order.
chapters.subtopics: Feedback policies; state and belief updates; receding-horizon control; model-predictive control; Bayesian learning; uncertain parameters; robust and distributionally robust optimization; dual control; changing volume, volatility, spread, and alpha; stability; excessive switching; hysteresis; guardrails; emergency completion; value of adaptation.

chapters.title: Passive Execution and Queue Control
chapters.purpose: Values a resting order as a contingent execution whose apparent spread saving must be balanced against non-fill and adverse-selection risk.
chapters.subtopics: Posting versus crossing; queue priority and position; fill probability; queue depletion; cancellation and reposting; conditional markouts; adverse selection after fills; survival and hazard models; marked point processes; non-fill and deadline risk; impulse control; aggressiveness selection.

chapters.title: Routing, Dark Liquidity, and Auctions
chapters.purpose: Extends the action from trading speed to venue, order type, and trading mechanism.
chapters.subtopics: Fragmented liquidity; fees and rebates; latency; fill quality; venue-specific toxicity; dark pools and conditional liquidity; information leakage; price protection; contextual bandits; constrained routing; opening and closing auctions; imbalance information; crossing opportunities; joint control of schedule, aggressiveness, and venue.

chapters.title: Futures Execution
chapters.purpose: Treats contract choice, roll dynamics, and economic exposure as part of the execution decision rather than as data-cleaning details.
chapters.subtopics: Contract multipliers, tick sizes, and risk-equivalent quantity; margin versus exposure; contract liquidity measures; front and deferred contracts; liquidity migration; roll timing; basis and calendar spreads; outright versus spread execution; continuous-series distortions; session boundaries; expiry effects; roll-aware impact models; two-expiry control; underestimation near rolls.

parts.title: Part IV - Determining whether a policy works
parts.purpose: A policy must be evaluated as a policy. These chapters separate genuine improvement from changes in order mix, market conditions, or the algorithm's own selection behavior.

chapters.title: Experiments and Policy Evaluation
chapters.purpose: Develops credible ways to decide whether a new execution policy improves outcomes and for which orders it improves them.
chapters.subtopics: Randomized execution experiments; A/B tests and switchbacks; stratification; interference; selection into algorithms; completion bias and censoring; common support; counterfactual policy values; inverse-propensity weighting; doubly robust estimation; heterogeneous effects; uncertainty for policy differences; economic versus statistical significance; staged rollout and monitoring.

chapters.title: Reinforcement Learning for Execution
chapters.purpose: Examines when execution should be treated as a learned sequential policy and why offline data make that problem difficult.
chapters.subtopics: MDPs and partially observed MDPs; state, action, transition, and reward design; inventory and deadline constraints; simulator construction; simulator bias; behavior policies; offline reinforcement learning; off-policy evaluation; distribution shift; conservative policy improvement; safe exploration; policy guardrails; comparison with model-predictive control.

parts.title: Part V - Other trading problems through the control lens
parts.purpose: The same language of state, belief, action, cost, and feedback is applied to other central problems in algorithmic trading.

chapters.title: Market Making and Inventory Control
chapters.purpose: Studies bid and ask decisions when the trader earns spread but accumulates inventory and adverse-selection risk.
chapters.subtopics: Reservation prices; Avellaneda-Stoikov; inventory penalties; quote skew; order-arrival calibration; fill probabilities; adverse selection; queue-aware quoting; volatility and regime changes; latency; multi-asset inventory; practical limits of stylized models.

chapters.title: Multi-Asset and Portfolio Execution
chapters.purpose: Coordinates the liquidation of related positions when risk, liquidity, and impact are coupled across instruments.
chapters.subtopics: Basket execution; covariance and factor risk; factor liquidity; cross-impact; coupled schedules; hedging during execution; index rebalances; portfolio transitions; manipulation-free cross-impact; parameter estimation; robustness to unstable correlations and liquidity.

chapters.title: Portfolio Choice with Trading Frictions
chapters.purpose: Connects forecasts and desired positions to the costly, gradual process of moving an actual portfolio.
chapters.subtopics: Signals and expected returns; turnover; transaction costs; signal decay; dynamic mean-variance control; no-trade regions; impulse and singular control; model-predictive rebalancing; robust portfolios; execution-aware portfolio construction; the boundary between portfolio and execution decisions.

chapters.title: Optimal Stopping and Statistical Arbitrage
chapters.purpose: Develops entry, exit, and abandonment decisions when waiting changes both information and opportunity.
chapters.subtopics: Stopping times; continuation value; Snell envelopes and dynamic programming; free-boundary intuition; mean-reverting spreads; pairs and relative-value models; regime uncertainty; sequential testing; transaction costs; delayed execution; signal decay; when a statistically attractive trade is not economically worth taking.

chapters.title: Options Hedging under Frictions
chapters.purpose: Studies hedging when rebalancing is discrete, costly, and itself moves the market.
chapters.subtopics: Delta and gamma exposure; discrete hedging error; stochastic volatility; transaction costs; impact-aware rebalancing; inventory constraints; no-trade regions; volatility and jump risk; joint hedge and execution decisions; liquidity differences across strikes and maturities.

chapters.title: Strategic Traders and Stochastic Games
chapters.purpose: Explains when market response depends on the beliefs and actions of other strategic participants, not only on exogenous noise.
chapters.subtopics: Signaling through order flow; strategic liquidation; predatory trading; information leakage; equilibrium impact; best responses; stochastic differential games; mean-field games; competition among execution algorithms; mechanism design; limits of single-agent control models.

parts.title: Part VI - Conducting execution research
parts.purpose: The final part brings the statistical, economic, and control ideas together in complete research workflows.

chapters.title: From Research Question to Production Model
chapters.purpose: Follows a model from its first research question through deployment, monitoring, and communication with traders and engineers.
chapters.subtopics: Problem statements and decision context; simple benchmarks; exploratory analysis; preregistered validation; reproducible experiments; feature and model versioning; leakage controls; stress and sensitivity tests; translating estimates into policy behavior; model-engine interfaces; monitoring and drift; retraining; governance; rollback; communicating uncertainty.

chapters.title: Worked Research Studies
chapters.purpose: Presents complete investigations so the reader can see how the book's principles interact when the data and conclusions are imperfect.
chapters.subtopics: Estimating an equity impact curve; diagnosing time-of-day effects; estimating transient-impact decay; designing and evaluating adaptive POV; modeling passive fills and adverse selection; futures execution around a roll; reproducing Almgren-Chriss and a propagator model; comparing a learned policy with a controlled baseline.
